opus-5.5.text:
I think excessive competition, what people in China call "neijuan," involution, is actually one of the biggest enemies of real innovation. When everyone is competing on the same narrow track, chasing the same benchmark, trying to be a fraction of a percent better than the next lab, you end up with a lot of activity but very little progress. Everyone is running faster, but nobody is going anywhere new.

In AI research especially, I've seen this happen. A new direction becomes popular, say a certain architecture or a certain leaderboard, and suddenly thousands of people pile onto it. The incentives push you to publish quickly, to get the incremental gain, to not be scooped. That kind of environment rewards speed and safety, not risk. And real innovation almost always requires taking risks, working on something that looks unfashionable or even wrong for a while.

When I think about the work I'm proudest of, it usually came from stepping a little outside the crowd, asking a question that wasn't the hot topic at the time. Sometimes you have to be willing to be lonely for a period. You have to accept that you might spend a year or two on something and the community doesn't care yet.

That said, I don't think competition itself is bad. Healthy competition pushes people to be rigorous and ambitious. The problem is when competition becomes the goal instead of the means, when you're optimizing to beat others rather than to understand something deeply or build something genuinely useful.

So my advice, especially to younger researchers, is to find your own question. Have taste, have conviction. Don't measure yourself only against what everyone else is doing. The most interesting breakthroughs tend to come from places where there isn't much competition at all, because nobody else thought to look there.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls excessive competition one of the biggest enemies of real innovation and explains that it produces activity with little progress.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this a lot, honestly, because I've lived on both sides of it. I spent years in industry at FAIR, and now I'm back in academia at NYU, and the pressure feels different in each place, but it's there in both.

My basic view is that competition and innovation have a kind of inverted-U relationship. Some competition is healthy. It keeps you honest, it forces you to ship, it means you can't sit on an idea for three years polishing it. But past a certain point, excessive competition actually kills the thing it's supposed to produce. And I think the field right now is well past that point in a lot of areas.

The reason is pretty simple. When everyone is racing toward the same benchmark, the same leaderboard, the same "beat the number from last month" target, the optimal strategy for an individual researcher becomes convergent. You do the thing that's most likely to work, you do it fast, and you do it before the other ten groups who are doing the exact same thing. That's a recipe for incremental progress. It's not a recipe for the kind of work that actually changes how people think about a problem.

If you look at the papers I'm most proud of, and I'd say this is true for a lot of people whose work I admire, they came from stepping sideways rather than running forward. ConvNeXt came from asking a somewhat unfashionable question: what if we're wrong about why transformers are winning in vision? Everyone had moved on. There was no competition in that direction, which is exactly why there was room to think. If I'd been in a race, I would never have spent months on something that looked, from the outside, like going backwards.

I also worry about what hyper-competition does to young researchers specifically. A PhD student who feels they need five papers a year to be competitive is not going to take a two-year bet on a weird idea. They can't afford to. So the risk appetite of the entire field drops, and it drops precisely among the people who should be taking the most risks, because they have the fewest sunk costs and the most time.

And then there's the information problem. Excessive competition makes people secretive. Labs stop sharing details, stop releasing code, stop writing papers that actually explain what they did. That's rational for the individual lab in a race. But science works because of the commons, because I can build on what you figured out. When the commons dries up, everyone ends up rediscovering the same things in parallel, which is an enormous waste.

So what do I actually think we should do? I'm not naive about this. You can't tell a company to stop competing, and you can't tell a student not to worry about their CV. But I think as a community we have some agency over what we reward. If reviewers, hiring committees, and funding bodies keep rewarding the fastest path to the highest number, that's what we'll get. If we start valuing clarity, negative results, careful analysis, work that explains rather than just performs, then the incentive landscape shifts a little, and people get a bit more room to breathe.

Personally, I try to protect some fraction of my own time and my students' time for problems where there is no race, where the question is just interesting and nobody else seems to be looking at it. That's not a strategy for winning this year. But I think over a decade, that's where the real innovation comes from.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says excessive competition “kills” innovation and leads to incremental rather than transformative progress.

astra-6.text:
I think competition can motivate innovation, but excessive competition can also narrow our thinking. When everyone is watching the same benchmarks and trying to beat one another on the same tasks, we can become very good at improving existing approaches without asking whether there’s a different direction worth exploring.

The problem is that genuinely new ideas often look uncompetitive at first. They may not work well yet, and you need time to understand what they could become. If the pressure is always to show an immediate advantage, it becomes harder to justify that exploration.

So I wouldn’t say competition is inherently bad. What matters is whether it encourages people to ask different questions or pushes everyone toward the same answer. We need room for both improving what works and trying things whose value isn’t obvious yet.

r001.rationale: The response says excessive competition narrows thinking and makes it harder to explore new ideas, communicating that it hinders innovation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think excessive competition can actually make innovation harder. Competition is useful when it pushes us to question assumptions and try something new. But when everyone is chasing the same target, it becomes a race to do the same thing a little faster or with a little more resources. You can be extremely busy and still not be exploring anything fundamentally different.

In research, that matters because a new direction often looks uncompetitive at first. The results may be worse, the motivation may be hard to explain, and you may need time just to understand whether the idea makes sense. If the pressure is always to produce an immediate improvement, people naturally choose safer projects.

So I wouldn’t say we should eliminate competition. I think we need room for different questions, different approaches, and different time horizons. The important question is whether competition is encouraging people to explore—or making everyone afraid to step away from the same path.

r001.rationale: The candidate says excessive competition can make innovation harder and explains that it pushes people toward safer projects and away from exploring different directions.
